"Vulgarize" has two meanings. They are connected by one shared idea — the idea of making something more common — but they work in different directions. Let me explain both carefully.

The first (and more common) meaning: to make something crude, cheap, or tasteless

When you vulgarize something, you take something that was once dignified, elegant, or artistically valuable — and you drag it down. You strip away its quality, refinement, or good taste and replace it with something crude, indecent, or cheap.

Picture a beautiful, serious piece of classical music. Now imagine someone remixing it purely for shock value — adding crude sound effects, turning it into a cheap parody, destroying every trace of artistry. That person has vulgarized the music. They took something elevated and reduced it to something crass.

Another example: when advertisers take a famous painting like the Mona Lisa and slap it on a product label to sell something cheap and unrelated, many people feel this vulgarizes the work. It robs the painting of its dignity and turns it into something commercial and tasteless.

So in this first sense, to vulgarize something means to corrupt or cheapen it — to lower its moral, aesthetic, or artistic quality through crudeness or poor taste.

A few clear example sentences: "The director vulgarized the classic novel by replacing its deep themes with crude humor." Or: "The comedian vulgarized the serious political debate by turning every question into a dirty joke."

The second (older, more literary) meaning: to make something accessible to ordinary people

This meaning is less common in everyday speech today, but it's important to know. In this sense, to vulgarize something means to take knowledge or an idea that is complex, technical, or understood only by experts — and explain or present it in a way that ordinary, everyday people can understand.

Think of a physicist who writes a popular book explaining black holes for non-scientists. She is vulgarizing astrophysics — bringing it out of the lab and into living rooms. Or think of a teacher who takes a dense philosophical text and rewrites it in plain, everyday language. He is vulgarizing philosophy.

This meaning can be neutral or even positive when the goal is to democratize knowledge and make it available to everyone. But it can also carry a faint note of criticism — the suggestion that in making something widely accessible, you inevitably lose some of its depth, nuance, or precision. So if someone says "that TV documentary vulgarizes evolutionary biology," they might mean it made the subject accessible — but at the cost of oversimplifying it.

Example sentences: "His bestselling book did much to vulgarize the discoveries of modern physics." Or: "The encyclopedia was written to vulgarize science for a general audience."

At first, these two meanings can seem completely different. But they share one core idea: both involve taking something elevated and making it more common.

In the first meaning, you make something morally or aesthetically common — you lower its quality down to the level of crudeness. In the second meaning, you make something intellectually common — you bring it down from the rarefied world of experts to the level of ordinary people. In both cases, something that was "above" gets brought down to everyday ground.

The difference lies in what is being lowered. In Meaning 1, it's the quality and dignity of something that gets reduced — and that is always negative. In Meaning 2, it's the complexity and exclusivity of something that gets reduced — and that can be a good thing or a bad thing depending on how carefully it's done.
Which meaning will you encounter more often?

In modern everyday English, the first meaning — making something crude or indecent — is by far the dominant one. If you hear someone use "vulgarize" in conversation without any special context, they almost certainly mean this first sense. The second meaning (to simplify and popularize for the general public) is more formal and literary; you're more likely to see it in essays, book reviews, academic writing, or older texts.

The noun form is vulgarization — the act or outcome of vulgarizing something. ("The vulgarization of art is a common complaint among critics.") The adjective and past tense form is vulgarized. ("The vulgarized version of the opera was barely recognizable.") Someone who vulgarizes something can be called a vulgarizer, though this word is rarely used.
